```bash
mitmdump -nr run.mitm --set flow_detail=2 '~d "uxcam|smartlook|clarity|fullstory|quantummetric|contentsquare|glassbox|logrocket"' | tee "$E/logs/D20-018-replay-flows.txt"; echo "output lines: $(grep -c '^' "$E/logs/D20-018-replay-flows.txt") (0 = no replay-vendor host in this capture)"
# replay payloads are gzipped frames/hierarchies: run the D20-024 inflate pass on those bodies before judging them opaque
```
items.proof:
The vendor dashboard replay — or the captured upload payload — showing the typed card number,
CVV, OTP or document image. Screenshot the replay with the value visible, next to the app screen.
items.escalation:
The SDK's dashboard is now a secondary data store holding cardholder and authentication
data; ask about its access control in the report. A replay URL exposed on a JS bridge is also a D10
finding. For a payments app, frame it as PCI-relevant -> D23.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every sensitive screen is registered with the SDK's occlusion API (show the call sites)
**and** a typed marker PAN does not appear in the uploaded payload or the dashboard replay. Screenshot the
masked replay — it is one of the few visually provable negatives in this chapter.

items.title: Per-SDK egress attribution — which class opened the socket
items.severity_note: High (the attribution is what makes the payload finding actionable)
items.attacker: AM-08
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0318 (References to SDK APIs Known to Handle Sensitive User Data), MASTG-TEST-0319 (Runtime Use of…), MASTG-TEST-0206 (which explicitly gives no code locations — pair the two); Google Play "Using SDKs safely and securely" (developers must treat SDK collection as their own and verify SDKs "implement logic respecting user consent preferences"); Oversecured SDK-security research on SDKs "collecting undisclosed data"; T1646
items.test:
"The app talks to eleven hosts" is an inventory. "This analytics SDK sent this user's email and
precise location" is a finding. Attribute every outbound URL to the stack that requested it, then join that
to the payload contents.
items.proof:
A table: `host | owning SDK (from the stack trace) | fields sent | user flow`. A row containing
an email, precise location, phone number, or a health/finance value going to a third-party host the privacy
policy does not name is the finding.
items.escalation:
-> D20-025 (compare against the Data safety declaration); -> D20-020 (run it again with
consent off); -> D18 (the SDK's own backend).
items.ruled_out_when:
Every third-party host in the capture receives only non-identifying telemetry (event
names, app version, coarse locale), attributed by stack trace, the payload sweep for the marker set
returns zero across a full flow pass, and the per-UID capture's flow count matches the proxy-based count (no
proxy-bypassing SDK) or the difference is attributed. Attach the host→SDK→fields table with the zero column.

items.title: The consent-off differential — identical traffic with every toggle off
items.vrt: `privacy_concerns.unnecessary_data_collection` (varies; the only concrete child, `…wifi_ssid_password`, is P4) — escalate via `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies)
items.attacker: AM-08
items.applies_to: all apps with a consent banner, a "do not sell/share" toggle, or a privacy-settings screen
items.maps_to: Google Play "Using SDKs safely and securely" (SDKs must "implement logic respecting user consent preferences"); MASWE-0073, MASWE-0074; MASVS-PRIVACY-1; the Body-Diff Rule (a byte-identical response is not a bypass — here, a byte-identical **capture** is the control failure)
items.test:
The single most convincing privacy test, and it takes two captures. Run one identical flow with
every consent toggle **on**, and one with every toggle **off**, from a freshly installed app each time.
Diff the host set and the field set. If the captures are equivalent, the toggle is decorative — that is a
demonstrable control failure, not a compliance opinion, and it is exactly the framing Intigriti's triage
standard requires.
items.how:
```bash
# run A: accept everything.  run B: decline everything.  Same flow, same account shape, fresh install each.
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell pm clear $PKG && mitmdump -w +consent_on.mitm    # ... drive flow, accept all ...
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell pm clear $PKG && mitmdump -w +consent_off.mitm   # ... drive flow, decline all ...
for f in consent_on consent_off; do
  mitmdump -nr $f.mitm -s /dev/stdin <<'PY' > $f.hosts
def request(f): print(f.request.pretty_host, f.request.path.split('?')[0])
PY
  echo "$f flows: $(wc -l < $f.hosts)"
done
diff <(sort -u consent_on.hosts) <(sort -u consent_off.hosts)
# field-level: does the same marker still leave?
for f in consent_on consent_off; do
  echo -n "$f marker hits: "; mitmdump -nr $f.mitm --set flow_detail=3 2>/dev/null | grep -c zq4h7m2kx9
done
```
items.proof:
The `diff` showing an empty or near-empty delta, plus equal marker counts in both runs, plus a
screenshot of the consent screen with the toggle in the off position. Quantify: *"11 of 11 third-party
hosts contacted with consent declined; the advertising ID and the account email left the device in both
runs."*
items.escalation:
-> D20-021 if collection also precedes the dialog; -> D20-025 for the declaration side;
-> D18 to name the SDK that ignored the flag.
items.ruled_out_when:
The consent-off run contacts a strict subset of hosts, the marker count drops to zero
for every optional data type, and the remaining hosts are first-party and functionally necessary. Keep the
`diff` output — a non-empty delta in the right direction is the negative.

items.title: Pre-consent transmission — data leaving before the dialog is dismissed
items.attacker: AM-08
items.applies_to: all apps that show a consent, ToS or privacy dialog on first launch
items.maps_to: MASWE-0073; MASWE-0071 (Inadequate Defaults for Privacy Relevant Actions); MASVS-PRIVACY-1; hackwithsingh sec-14-18 #15 "logs user location data without proper consent", #25, #30; riya78 §7
items.test:
Pre-consent transmission is the step that converts a hygiene note into a reportable finding — the
app has not merely collected more than it declared, it has processed before any lawful basis existed.
Analytics SDKs initialise in `Application.onCreate()`, which runs before the first Activity draws.
items.how:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell pm clear $PKG
mitmdump -w +firstlaunch.mitm &
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -n $PKG/.MainActivity
# DO NOT TOUCH THE DEVICE. wait 30s with the consent dialog still on screen.
sleep 30; kill %1
mitmdump -nr firstlaunch.mitm -s /dev/stdin <<'PY'
def request(f):
    print(f.request.timestamp_start, f.request.pretty_host, f.request.path[:70], len(f.request.content or b''))
PY
# what identifiers went with it?
AID=$(adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings get secure android_id | tr -d '\r')
mitmdump -nr firstlaunch.mitm --set flow_detail=3 2>/dev/null | grep -c "$AID"
```
items.proof:
A timestamped request to a third-party host sent **before** the consent dialog was dismissed,
carrying the Android ID / advertising ID / precise location — with a screen recording showing the dialog
still on screen at that timestamp.
items.escalation:
-> D20-020 (the toggle is also decorative); -> D03 if a permission was requested and used
before any user-facing rationale.
items.ruled_out_when:
The first-launch capture contains only first-party calls required to render the consent
screen itself (config, strings, feature flags) and no identifier from the sweep in D20-052 to D20-054.
Attach the timestamped host list.

items.title: `AppOpsManager.OnOpNotedCallback` — make the app confess its own private-data reads
items.severity_note: High (as evidence for an undeclared-collection report)
items.attacker: n/a — instrumentation that produces the strongest evidence in this chapter
items.applies_to: **Android 11+ (API 30+)**; `<attribution android:tag>` is required for targetSdk 31+
items.maps_to: developer.android.com/guide/topics/data/audit-access — `AppOpsManager.OnOpNotedCallback`, `onNoted(SyncNotedAppOp)`, `onSelfNoted(SyncNotedAppOp)`, `onAsyncNoted(AsyncNotedAppOp)`, `setOnOpNotedCallback(mainExecutor, cb)`, `SyncNotedAppOp.op` / `.attributionTag`, `AsyncNotedAppOp.getMessage()`; MASTG-TEST-0319
items.test:
The platform will tell you which code read the user's private data — including code inside
bundled SDKs — with attribution tags and stack traces. Inject the callback with Frida and you get an
authoritative, first-party record of every location, contacts, camera and microphone access, attributed to
the calling class. This is far stronger evidence than a grep.
items.proof:
Stack traces naming a **third-party package** as the caller of a location/contacts/camera read,
with the op name and attribution tag, correlated to a request body in the proxy.
items.escalation:
-> D18 SDK accountability; -> D20-025 for the declaration mismatch; -> D03 if the
permission exists only because an SDK's manifest merged it in.
items.ruled_out_when:
Across a full functional pass the callback reports only ops the app's own packages
perform, each tied to a user-initiated action, with attribution tags that match the feature — and only if
`[opcb] installed` printed and a user-initiated location/camera read produced an `[noted]` line (positive
control). Save the op log; an empty third-party column is the negative.

items.title: Attribution-tag mismatch — the Privacy Dashboard shows the wrong reason
items.attacker: n/a — transparency defect
items.applies_to: **targetSdk 31+**
items.maps_to: developer.android.com/guide/topics/data/audit-access — *"A `null` attribution tag indicates the main part of your app"*; `<attribution android:tag="sharePhotos" android:label="@string/share_photos_attribution_label" />`; MASVS-PRIVACY-1
items.test:
Attribution tags feed the system's access records, which the user sees in the Privacy Dashboard.
An app that performs every read under the default (null) attribution, or under a tag whose label does not
describe the actual purpose, presents the user with an inaccurate account of why their data was accessed.
items.how:
```bash
grep -n '<attribution' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
# map tag -> user-visible label
python3 - <<'PY'
import re,sys
m=open('$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml').read()
for t,l in re.findall(r'<attribution[^>]*android:tag="([^"]+)"[^>]*android:label="([^"]+)"',m):
    print(t,'->',l)
PY
```
Then collect `attributionTag` per op with the D20-022 hook and compare.
items.proof:
A background location read reported under a tag labelled "Share photos", or under no tag at all
while the app declares several attributions.
items.escalation: Pair with D20-022 into one undeclared/misattributed-collection report.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every op the callback reports carries a tag whose declared label matches the feature
that triggered it, or the app declares no attributions at all and performs all reads from a single
user-initiated feature (in which case the null tag is accurate).

items.title: Archived or encrypted telemetry batches — hook the pre-compression boundary
items.vrt: rate on what the decoded payload contains
items.attacker: n/a — instrumentation
items.applies_to: all; standard for high-volume analytics SDKs
items.maps_to: T1532 Archive Collected Data (ATT&CK: BRATA S1094 "compressed data with the `zlib` library before exfiltration"; Exodus "encrypts data using XOR prior to exfiltration"); T1646 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel; MASTG-TECH-0100
items.test:
When a telemetry batch is gzipped, protobuf-encoded or encrypted before upload, the proxy shows
you an opaque blob and the privacy review stops there. Do not fight the format — hook the boundary just
before it.
items.proof:
The decompressed or pre-encryption payload printed by the hook, containing PII the app never
disclosed it collects, matched to the opaque upload in the proxy by size and timestamp.
items.escalation: Feeds D20-019 and D20-025; the archiving itself is Low, the contents carry the rating.
items.ruled_out_when:
The pre-compression hook fires (prove it) and the decoded batches contain only event
names, counters and non-identifying context across a full flow pass.

items.title: Undeclared PII on the wire versus the Play Data safety declaration
items.severity_note: High (Critical where it is multi-user sensitive PII per the HackerOne standard)
items.attacker: AM-08 (a third-party recipient) — for a first-party-only flow this is a compliance finding, which most bounty programmes route to a privacy track rather than pay
items.applies_to: all apps handling user data
items.maps_to: MASWE-0072 (Inadequate Privacy Policy); MASTG-TEST-0206 (Undeclared PII in Network Traffic Capture) — the test fails *"if you can find the PII you entered in the app that is not declared in the app's marketplace privacy declarations (e.g. Data Safety section in Google Play) and/or in its privacy policy"*; prerequisites `identify-sensitive-data`, `privacy-policy`, `app-store-privacy-declarations`; MASTG-TECH-0100; MASTG-TOOL-0097 (mitmproxy), MASTG-TOOL-0077 (Burp), MASTG-TOOL-0079 (ZAP), MASTG-TOOL-0081 (Wireshark); MASWE-0073 (Inadequate Data Collection Declarations), MASWE-0074 (Inadequate Tracking Domains Declarations); MASVS-PRIVACY-1, MASVS-PRIVACY-3; OWASP Mobile Top 10 2024 M6; CWE-359
items.test:
The evaluation is a compliance **delta**, not a judgement: capture decrypted traffic while
entering the marker set from D20-002, then compare what leaves against the Play listing's Data safety
section and the privacy policy. MASTG is explicit that this test yields no code locations — pair it with
D20-019 / MASTG-TEST-0318-0319 to name the SDK and call site, which is what makes it actionable.
items.how:
```bash
mitmdump -w +traffic.flows --set connection_strategy=lazy &
# exercise every flow, typing the canaries
mitmdump -nr traffic.flows -s /dev/stdin <<'PY'
NEEDLES = [b'zq4h7m2kx9', b'zq4h7m2kx9@example.invalid', b'15550137742', b'1970-01-01', b'zk8v3p1nd6']
def response(f):
    body = (f.request.content or b'') + (f.response.content or b'') + f.request.pretty_url.encode()
    for n in NEEDLES:
        if n in body:
            print(f.request.pretty_host, f.request.path[:70], n.decode())
PY
```
MASTG ships an equivalent `mitm_sensitive_logger.py` whose core is a `SENSITIVE_DATA` dict of marker
values, a `contains_sensitive_data()` check over URL / request body / response body, and an append to
`sensitive_data.log`, wired into both `def request(flow)` and `def response(flow)`.
Then pull the declaration side:
```bash
# the Data safety section is on the Play listing; record data types + "shared with third parties"
# and the privacy policy URL from the same listing
aapt2 d badging app.apk | grep -i -E 'package:|versionName'
```
items.proof:
A `sensitive_data.log`-shaped entry showing the marker leaving the device to a named host, side
by side with the app's published Data safety declaration that omits that data type or that recipient —
e.g.
```
REQUEST URL: https://collector.example-analytics.com/v2/e
Request Body: uid=…&email=zq4h7m2kx9%40example.invalid&lat=51.5074&lon=-0.1278
```
with the listing declaring neither "Email address" nor "Approximate/precise location" as shared.
items.escalation:
-> D28-047 when the undeclared data is a prompt, chat history or attachment sent to a model host (owned there); -> D20-019 to name the SDK; -> D20-020 if consent toggles do not change it; -> D18 if the
recipient's backend is itself misconfigured. Frame it as data exposure to an unauthorised party with a
concrete captured payload — **never as a compliance argument**, which Intigriti's standard rejects
outright.
items.ruled_out_when:
A full-flow capture with the marker set produces hits only on first-party hosts, for
data types the Data safety section declares as collected, with no third-party recipient. Attach the
host × data-type matrix with the declaration column filled in.

items.title: PII placed in URL query parameters, and the referer consequence
items.severity_note: Medium (High for a session or reset token)
items.applies_to: all apps with a remote backend; the WebView half applies to any in-app browser
items.maps_to: OWASP Mobile Top 10 2024 M6 — *"URL query parameters: Data visible in server logs and browser history"*; MASWE-0073; MASVS-PRIVACY-3
items.test:
(D20-015 owns the query-string sweep and the log copy; this item adds only the Referer consequence and the WebView half — one capture, two VRT rows.) A value in a query string is copied into CDN logs, proxy logs, WebView history and — if the URL
is loaded in a WebView with third-party resources — the `Referer` header sent to each of them. The
remediation to state is exactly M6's: move the value into the POST body or a header.
items.how:
Use the mitmproxy query-key sweep from D20-015, then check the WebView half:
```bash
grep -rnE 'loadUrl\(|loadDataWithBaseURL|CustomTabsIntent|setAcceptThirdPartyCookies' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# capture what the WebView sends as Referer to third-party hosts on that page
mitmdump -nr run.mitm -s /dev/stdin <<'PY'
def request(f):
    r = f.request.headers.get('referer')
    if r and ('token' in r or 'zq4h7m2kx9' in r):
        print(f.request.pretty_host, '<- Referer:', r[:120])
PY
```
items.proof:
A full URL containing PII or a token in the query string; and, for the referer variant, a
request to a third-party host whose `Referer` carries it.
items.escalation: -> D10 (WebView history and referer); -> D13 if the token is a reset or session token.
items.ruled_out_when:
No authenticated or identifying value appears in any query string across the flow set,
and no `Referer` to a third-party host contains one. Report the suspect-key sweep's zero count.

items.title: Fat profile endpoints returning fields the app never renders
items.severity_note: Critical (recovery codes, password hashes, auth tokens) down to Medium (excess PII)
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies); a recovery-code dump chains to `broken_authentication_and_session_management.two_fa_bypass` (P3) or `…authentication_bypass` (P1)
items.attacker: AM-05 (own account, own token — then escalate cross-user via D15)
items.applies_to: all mobile backends
items.maps_to: `hunt-mfa-bypass` recovery-code dump; `hunt-graphql` field-level authorisation; `triage-validation` anti-patterns list; CWE-200
items.test:
The mobile client displays three fields; the API returns forty — including recovery codes,
internal flags, moderation notes, and other users' identifiers. **The calibration matters:** "the API
returns more fields than necessary" is an anti-pattern that loses money unless the extra fields are
actually sensitive. Name the field and why it is sensitive, or do not file it.
items.how:
```bash
# 1. what does the UI render? (from the layout and the model class)
# jadx emits Java: a Kotlin `data class` decompiles to a class with copy()/componentN(), never the `data class` keyword
grep -rlE 'public final [A-Za-z<>]+ copy\(|component1\(\)' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | xargs grep -lE 'class (User|Profile|Account|Me|Customer)\b' | head
# list that class's fields, then grep the getters' call sites in Activity/Fragment/Compose classes for the rendered set (getEmail\(\)|\.email\b)
# 2. what does the API actually return?
curl -s https://api.target.example/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $A" | jq 'keys'
curl -s https://api.target.example/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $A" \
  | jq -r 'paths(scalars) as $p | "\($p|join("."))"' | sort
# 3. cross-check the spec for fields no screen uses
jq -r '.components.schemas | keys[]' openapi.json 2>/dev/null
```
items.proof:
The response body with the sensitive fields named — recovery codes, a password hash, an
internal role flag, another user's identifier — and, for the cross-user case, the same fields retrieved
with a second account's token (marker-verified).
items.escalation:
-> D13 if recovery codes or an MFA secret are present (that is an MFA bypass, filed
separately); -> D15 for the field-level authorisation and IDOR directions.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every field in the response is either rendered by some screen or non-sensitive
(timestamps, feature flags, display preferences). List the unrendered fields and why each is benign —
that list is the negative.

items.title: Authenticated responses cacheable, and cached on disk
items.attacker: AM-05 (a shared device), AM-04 where the cache is reachable — AM-12 to observe (the root read of the sandbox is evidence, never the precondition)
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: sehno "Test for cache management on HTTP (eg Pragma, Expires, Max-age)"; MASTG-TEST-0320 (WebViews Not Cleaning Up Sensitive Data) for the WebView cache half; CWE-524
items.test:
Two halves. Server side: does a PII-bearing response carry `Cache-Control: no-store`? Client
side: does the app's own HTTP cache (OkHttp `Cache`, WebView cache) keep the body on disk after logout?
items.how:
```bash
curl -sI -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" https://api.target.example/v1/me | grep -iE 'cache-control|pragma|expires|vary'
AS 'ls -la cache/ files/ app_webview/Default 2>/dev/null'              # AS(): root read of the sandbox (## Items); run-as only works on a debuggable build
AS 'grep -rl "zq4h7m2kx9" cache/ files/ 2>/dev/null' | head
AS 'tar c app_webview/Default' > webview.tar && tar xf webview.tar     # AS() uses exec-out: no pty, the tar stream arrives intact
strings -n 6 "app_webview/Default/Local Storage/leveldb/"*.log 2>/dev/null | grep -aiE 'zq4h7m2kx9|token|email'
```
items.proof:
`Cache-Control: public` (or a missing `no-store`) on a PII response, and the same marker found
in the app's on-disk cache after logout.
items.escalation:
-> D15 web-cache deception if a shared cache is involved; -> D11 for the on-disk payload's
reachability; -> D20-060 if it survives logout.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every authenticated response carries `Cache-Control: no-store` (or `private, no-cache`
with a correct `Vary`), and a post-logout grep of `cache/`, `files/` and the WebView profile for the marker
returns zero across a non-zero file count.

items.title: Contacts and calendar harvesting on the invite / find-friends flow
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies) — this is third-party PII (the contacts themselves never consented)
items.attacker: AM-08; the data subjects are people who are not users of the app at all
items.applies_to: all apps with an invite, "find people you know", or contact-sync feature
items.maps_to: T1636.003 Protected User Data: Contact List; T1636.001 Calendar Entries; MASTG-TEST-0254 (Dangerous App Permissions), MASWE-0066 (Inadequate Permission Management — its MASTG test "Permission Requests Not Minimized" is a placeholder upstream); MASWE-0067 (Lack of Anonymisation or Pseudonymisation Measures); CWE-359
items.test:
Four questions, each a different finding: (a) is the **whole** address book uploaded or only the
contact the user picked; (b) is it uploaded **before** the user picks anyone; (c) are phone numbers hashed,
and if so, is the hash unsalted MD5/SHA-1 (trivially reversible across the phone-number keyspace); (d) is
the data retained server-side after the invite is sent.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ContactsContract|READ_CONTACTS|CalendarContract|READ_CALENDAR|CommonDataKinds\.(Phone|Email)|uploadContacts|syncContacts|hashPhone|normalizePhone' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# seed canary contacts, then proxy the invite flow
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content insert --uri content://com.android.contacts/raw_contacts \
  --bind account_name:s:canary --bind account_type:s:canary
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content insert --uri content://com.android.contacts/data \
  --bind raw_contact_id:i:1 --bind mimetype:s:vnd.android.cursor.item/name \
  --bind data1:s:zq4h7m2kx9
# then: open the invite screen and capture BEFORE tapping any contact
mitmdump -nr invite.mitm --set flow_detail=3 2>/dev/null | grep -c zq4h7m2kx9
# days later, is it still there?
curl -s https://api.target.example/v1/me/contacts -H "Authorization: Bearer $A" | jq 'length'
```
items.proof:
A request body containing the full address book captured **before** any contact was selected,
or unsalted phone hashes, plus a follow-up `GET` showing the data still present days later.
items.escalation:
Reversible phone hashes plus the user-search oracle in D15 is full social-graph
reconstruction. -> D20-025 if the Data safety section does not declare contacts.
items.ruled_out_when:
The upload contains only the contact the user explicitly selected, sent after
selection, with a salted/peppered identifier or no identifier at all, and a retention endpoint shows it
is not persisted. Capture the "before selection" flow list showing zero contact payloads.

items.title: Lock-screen notification content — visibility, channel override, and `setPublicVersion`
items.severity_note: High (an OTP on a locked screen is a second-factor bypass for anyone holding the device)
items.attacker: **AM-10** physical locked — the rare item where AM-10 is the primary model
items.applies_to: all. MASTG's evaluation uses **`minSdkVersion`**, not `targetSdkVersion`, because that "ensures the test accounts for the least secure environment in which the app can operate": it fails if sensitive data is exposed **and** (`minSdkVersion >= 33` with `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` declared) **or** (`minSdkVersion <= 32`, regardless of the permission)
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0315 (Sensitive Data Exposed via Notifications) — named data types "personally identifiable information (PII), one-time passwords (OTPs), or other sensitive data, like health or financial details"; MASWE-0037 (CWE-200, CWE-359); MASTG-KNOW-0054; the MASTG best practice "Preventing Sensitive Data Exposure in Notifications" (a placeholder upstream); semgrep rules `mastg-android-sensitive-data-in-notifications` and `…-manifest`; mobsfscan `android_sensitive_notification`; deprecated predecessor MASTG-TEST-0005; developer.android.com `develop/ui/views/notifications/build-notification` (`VISIBILITY_PUBLIC` / `VISIBILITY_PRIVATE` / `VISIBILITY_SECRET`, `setPublicVersion()`, channel `lockscreenVisibility`); T1517
items.test:
Three settings interact and developers get the precedence wrong. `VISIBILITY_PUBLIC` shows full
content on the keyguard; `VISIBILITY_PRIVATE` shows only basic info **and should be paired with
`setPublicVersion()`** or the system substitutes a generic line; `VISIBILITY_SECRET` shows nothing. The
**channel's** `lockscreenVisibility` can override the per-notification value, so check both.
items.how:

items.title: `NotificationListenerService` reading `Notification.extras` — build the PoC listener
items.severity_note: High (Critical when the value is an OTP that completes an account takeover)
items.attacker: **AM-04** — notification access is a single user toggle, no dangerous permission
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `reference/android/service/notification/NotificationListenerService` (`BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE`, `onNotificationPosted`, `getActiveNotifications()`, `Notification.extras`, `Notification.EXTRA_TEXT`, `contentIntent`); MASWE-0037; MASTG-TEST-0315; Google Mobile VRP Low Impact Data includes "content of a user's messages (email, instant messages, text messages)"; empirical: Mail.ru "read new emails from any inbox in notification center" **$10,000**; T1517 Access Notifications (ATT&CK: *"In the case of Credential Access, adversaries may attempt to intercept one-time code sent to the device"*; Escobar "steals Google Authenticator MFA codes"; SharkBot "intercepts notifications and leverages Direct Reply features"; mitigation: **Application Developer Guidance — avoid sensitive data in notification text**); T1644 Out of Band Data
items.test:
(Owner of the listener PoC; D06-048 covers the same listener from the service side and D08-040 the mutable-PendingIntent exploitation step — build the PoC once, here.) Lock-screen visibility settings are irrelevant here: a listener reads `Notification.extras`
regardless, including `EXTRA_TEXT`, `EXTRA_BIG_TEXT`, `EXTRA_TITLE`, every action's label, and the
`contentIntent` itself. The notification-access grant is a normal, user-facing toggle that banking
trojans routinely obtain, and it is the precondition you must state honestly.
items.proof:
Your PoC's own `poc.log` line (not only logcat) containing the OTP / message body / balance, with
the target's package name in the same line, plus a screenshot of the ordinary settings toggle the user flipped. State the
attacker app's permission set — ideally empty besides the listener binding.
items.escalation:
-> D09/D24 join: the listener also reads the notification's deep link and its extras, then
replays that deep link itself (see Cross-surface joins); -> D08 if the `contentIntent` is a mutable
`PendingIntent`; -> D13 for the OTP.
items.ruled_out_when:
The target's notifications carry no sensitive value in any `extras` key — the OTP is
delivered only in-app, the message body is replaced by "New message", the balance is omitted — verified by
the PoC listener logging only generic strings while `poc.log` holds the positive-control line from the benign
notification, proving the channel. Keep that log as the negative.

items.title: Android 15 OTP redaction for listeners, and the apps that route around it
items.attacker: AM-04
items.applies_to: **Android 15+**, all apps regardless of targetSdk
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `about/versions/15/behavior-changes-all` — *"Untrusted apps implementing `NotificationListenerService` cannot read unredacted OTP content from notifications. Trusted companion device associations exempt. System automatically redacts OTPs"*; T1517
items.test:
Android 15 redacts OTP content from untrusted listeners, with a carve-out for trusted
companion-device associations. Two findings live here. (a) The app under test *is* a listener and has been
built to obtain a `CompanionDeviceManager` association purely to keep reading OTPs. (b) The app under test
*sends* OTPs in a shape the redaction heuristic misses — the code in the title rather than the body, the
code split across an action label, the code in an accessibility node, or the code placed on the clipboard.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn -E 'BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE|NotificationListenerService' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rn -E 'CompanionDeviceManager|REQUEST_COMPANION_PROFILE|REQUEST_COMPANION_RUN_IN_BACKGROUND|associate\(' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml $DEC/jadx/sources/
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell cmd notification allow_listener com.poc/.Listener
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys notification | grep -iE 'listener|redact'
# trigger the target's OTP notification on an Android 15 device and read the PoC's log
adb -s "$SERIAL" logcat -s POC:E -d
```
items.proof:
The test listener receiving an **unredacted** 6-digit code on Android 15 from the target app —
which proves the app's OTP delivery falls outside the platform's redaction heuristics — or the target
holding a companion-device association whose only purpose is the exemption.
items.escalation:
-> D13 account takeover. On devices below Android 15, D20-031 already covers it; say which
API levels your claim applies to.
items.ruled_out_when:
On Android 15 the PoC listener receives the notification with the code replaced by the
redaction placeholder, and the code appears nowhere else (title, action label, clipboard, accessibility
tree). Test all four routes before writing the negative.

items.title: Notification history retains the content after dismissal
items.attacker: AM-11 physical unlocked, AM-05 shared device
items.applies_to: **Android 11+ (API 30+)** where the user has enabled notification history
items.maps_to: hackwithsingh sec-14-14 #48 "notification history accessible via settings reveals sensitive data", #42 "ticker text reveals sensitive information on status bar", #17 "big text style exposes full message content on lock screen"; MASWE-0037
items.test:
Dismissing a notification does not remove it. Android 11's notification history keeps recent
notifications in Settings, so an OTP or message body the user swiped away minutes ago is still readable by
whoever next picks up the unlocked device. Apps that rely on "the notification is transient" are wrong.
items.how:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings put secure notification_history_enabled 1
# trigger the notification, dismiss it, then:
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys notification --noredact | grep -iA6 -E 'history|HistoryArchive'
# and on device: Settings > Notifications > Notification history
adb -s "$SERIAL" exec-out screencap -p > nhistory.png
```
items.proof:
The dismissed OTP or message body still visible in notification history, screenshotted, with
the time elapsed since dismissal.
items.escalation: -> D20-030 (same root cause — sensitive text in the notification); -> D13.
items.ruled_out_when:
The app's sensitive notifications carry no sensitive text (so history retains nothing
useful), or the app posts them with `setLocalOnly`/`FLAG_ONLY_ALERT_ONCE` semantics and the history entry
shows only a generic line. Screenshot the history entry.

items.title: Notification content during screen sharing, and the default-recorder exemption
items.severity_note: High (for an OTP or message body)
items.attacker: AM-02 (a remote party on a support or casting session — the classic remote-access-scam vector)
items.applies_to: **Android 15+** for the platform protection; below that there is no protection at all
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `about/versions/15/behavior-changes-all` — "Notification content hidden during screen sharing"; `Notification.Builder.setPublicVersion()`; **"Default system screen recorder exempted"**
items.test:
Android 15 hides notification content during screen sharing and lets the app supply an
alternative via `setPublicVersion()`. An app that puts sensitive content in a notification and supplies no
public version is relying entirely on the platform's judgment — and the protection **does not apply to the
default system screen recorder**, which is exempted. Test with the built-in recorder, not a third-party
one, or you will report a false negative.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn -E 'setPublicVersion|VISIBILITY_PRIVATE|VISIBILITY_SECRET|setVisibility\(' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# start the BUILT-IN screen recorder (Quick Settings tile), then post the sensitive notification
# use the Quick Settings recorder or a cast/share session: `adb screenrecord` is not a MediaProjection consumer and never engages the protection (see D20-039 for the shell path)
adb -s "$SERIAL" pull /sdcard/r.mp4
```
items.proof:
The OTP, balance or message body visible in the default recorder's output, or in a screen-share
session recorded from the far end.
items.escalation: -> D20-038 (`setContentSensitivity` for the in-app view half); -> D13.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every sensitive notification supplies a `setPublicVersion()` whose text is generic, and
the recorded output shows only that generic line. Attach the frame.

items.title: `RemoteInput` / Direct Reply actions exposed on a sensitive notification
items.attacker: AM-04 (notification access)
items.applies_to: all apps posting notifications with actions
items.maps_to: T1517 Access Notifications (ATT&CK: SharkBot "intercepts notifications and leverages Direct Reply features"); developer.android.com `NotificationListenerService` (`Notification.Action.actionIntent`, `RemoteInput`)
items.test:
A notification listener does not only read — it can **fire** a notification's actions and fill a
`RemoteInput`. If any action performs a sensitive operation (reply to a chat, approve a login, confirm a
transfer, mark a transaction as recognised), notification access becomes an action primitive rather than a
read primitive.
items.proof:
The listener enumerating a sensitive action, then the action completing (a reply sent, an
approval recorded) with the server-side state change shown — run only against your own test account.
items.escalation:
-> D08 if the `actionIntent` is a mutable `PendingIntent` (then the listener also controls
its contents); -> D13 if the action approves a login.
items.ruled_out_when:
No notification carries an action that performs a state change without a further
in-app, authenticated confirmation — enumerate the action list and show each one opens a UI rather than
committing.

items.title: The screen-capture consumer inventory — decide who can capture before testing whether they can
items.vrt: `insecure_data_storage.screen_caching_enabled` (P5) is the trap node; the escalation is `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies)
items.attacker: AM-04 (MediaProjection or accessibility consumer), AM-08 (in-process SDK), AM-11 (physical)
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: T1513 Screen Capture (ATT&CK: *"Background applications can capture screenshots or videos of another application running in the foreground by using the Android `MediaProjectionManager` (generally requires the device user to grant consent)"*; mitigation *"Application developers can apply the `FLAG_SECURE` property to sensitive screens"*; *"An adversary with root access or Android Debug Bridge (adb) access could call the Android `screencap` or `screenrecord` commands"*); T1453; MASWE-0038
items.test:
"No `FLAG_SECURE`" is P5 (`screen_caching_enabled`) and Bugcrowd's own remediation text calls the
fix "a best practice". Before running any capture test, decide which of the five consumers you can actually
demonstrate, because the consumer decides the rating and, more importantly, the *route*:
1. **The system Recents snapshot** — D04-043 owns it; AM-11/AM-05, Low.
2. **`adb screencap` / `screenrecord`** — AM-11/AM-12; evidence-gathering, not an attack in itself.
3. **A `MediaProjection` consumer** — AM-04, one consent dialog; see D20-037.
4. **An in-process SDK capture** — AM-08, and **`FLAG_SECURE` does not stop it**; see D20-017, D20-018.
5. **A remote viewer on a screen share** — AM-02; see D20-034, D20-038.
Routes 4 and 5 are the ones nobody tests and the only ones that clear P5 reliably.
items.how:
```bash
# who is capable right now?
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys media_projection
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings get secure enabled_accessibility_services
grep -rn -E 'DETECT_SCREEN_CAPTURE|MediaProjection|FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROJECTION' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
# and what does the app itself do about it?
grep -rnE 'FLAG_SECURE|setContentSensitivity|setRecentsScreenshotEnabled|setFilterTouchesWhenObscured|registerScreenCaptureCallback|addScreenRecordingCallback' $DEC/jadx/sources/
```
items.proof:
A one-line statement in the report naming which consumer you demonstrated, with the artefact
from the corresponding item. Do not present `adb screencap` on your own rooted device as the attack.
items.escalation:
Play Integrity's `environmentDetails.appAccessRiskVerdict.appsDetected` names
`KNOWN_CAPTURING` / `UNKNOWN_CAPTURING` and `KNOWN_CONTROLLING` / `UNKNOWN_CONTROLLING` — that is the
vocabulary to use when arguing to a triager that the capturing consumer exists in the wild.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every sensitive screen sets `FLAG_SECURE` **and** an in-process capture path (crash
screenshot, session-replay frame) has been tested and produces a masked frame. `FLAG_SECURE` alone is not
a complete negative — route 4 goes around it.

items.title: `MediaProjection` per-session consent (Android 14) and the fallbacks apps chose instead
items.severity_note: High (persistent screen capture beyond the consent the user gave)
items.attacker: AM-04 for a third-party capturer; for the target app itself this is a covert-collection finding
items.applies_to: **targetSdk 34+** for the per-session rule; Android 15+ adds the status-bar chip and auto-stop on lock
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `about/versions/14/behavior-changes-14` — per-session consent, `SecurityException` on reusing a cached `createScreenCaptureIntent()` result, one `createVirtualDisplay()` per `MediaProjection`, mandatory `MediaProjection.Callback#onStop()` (otherwise `IllegalStateException`), `VirtualDisplay#resize()`/`setSurface()` for config changes; `about/versions/15/behavior-changes-all` — status-bar chip, "auto-stops when device screen locked"; `media/grow/media-projection`; T1513
items.test:
From targetSdk 34 an app can no longer cache the projection consent `Intent` and silently
re-capture. Two directions. (a) The target app still achieves silent repeat capture — it targets below 34,
or abuses an exemption. (b) The target app *used* to cache consent and, in the release that removed the
caching, fell back to something worse: a persistent `mediaProjection` foreground service kept alive across
what the user perceives as separate sessions, or an accessibility service.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'createScreenCaptureIntent|getMediaProjection|createVirtualDisplay|MediaProjection\.Callback|registerCallback|FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROJECTION' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
aapt2 d badging app.apk | grep targetSdkVersion
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys media_projection
adb -s "$SERIAL" logcat -d | grep -i 'SecurityException.*MediaProjection'
# is an FGS staying alive between sessions?
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys activity services $PKG | grep -iE 'mediaProjection|foreground|started'
```
items.proof:
A second capture session starting with **no** new consent dialog — screen-record the absence of
the prompt — or a `mediaProjection` FGS that persists across sessions, or an accessibility-service fallback
appearing in the same release that removed the caching (diff the two APK versions).
items.escalation: -> D06 foreground-service-type abuse; -> D20-065 if the capture is also concealed.
items.ruled_out_when:
`targetSdkVersion >= 34`, every capture session shows a fresh consent dialog, the
`MediaProjection.Callback` is registered, and the FGS stops when capture stops (`dumpsys activity services`
shows no lingering service).

items.title: `setContentSensitivity` / screen-share protection unused on payment and PIN views
items.attacker: AM-02 (the remote viewer in a support-call or casting scam)
items.applies_to: **Android 15+**, all apps
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `about/versions/15/behavior-changes-all` — screenshare protection, `Notification.Builder.setPublicVersion()`, `View.setContentSensitivity(int)`, Developer Options "Disable screen share protections", default system screen recorder exempted; `about/versions/16/…` for `accessibilityDataSensitive` (see D20-050); MASWE-0038
items.test:
Android 15 hides sensitive password input and OTP-bearing notification content from remote
viewers, and lets an app mark its own views with `View.setContentSensitivity(int)`. A payment, PIN or
recovery-phrase view that is neither `FLAG_SECURE` nor content-sensitivity-marked is fully visible to the
far end of a screen share — which is the mechanism of the current generation of remote-access support scams.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn -E 'setContentSensitivity|CONTENT_SENSITIVITY_SENSITIVE|FLAG_SECURE|setPublicVersion' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# reproduce the remote view with a REAL MediaProjection consumer — the PoC capturer from D20-037, a casting session, or a
# meeting app's share-screen. Never scrcpy or `adb screenrecord`: shell-level capture does not start a projection, so the
# protection is not engaged and the field is visible in every run (a built-in false positive)
# control: the stock password field must appear redacted in the same session before you judge the app's own views
# testing-only toggle (Android 15 Developer Options key), to confirm the protection is what is (or is not) acting:
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings put global disable_screen_share_protections_for_apps_and_notifications 1   # confirm the key: settings list global | grep screen_share
```
items.proof:
Side by side — the sensitive field visible in the projected stream, and the same field redacted
once `FLAG_SECURE` or sensitivity marking is applied in a patched build. State the Android version.
items.escalation: -> D20-034 for the notification half; -> D13 where the exposed field is a PIN or OTP.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every sensitive view is either `FLAG_SECURE` or marked content-sensitive, and the
projected stream shows it redacted on an Android 15 device. Capture the redacted frame.

items.title: Screenshot and screen-recording detection callbacks available but unused
items.severity_note: Medium (a missing control; High where the screen shows a full PAN, a recovery phrase or a one-time code)
items.vrt: `insecure_data_storage.screen_caching_enabled` (P5) for the capture itself; the missing control has no node of its own — argue it as a contributing factor
items.applies_to: **Android 14+** for screenshot detection, **Android 15+** for recording detection
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `about/versions/14/features/screenshot-detection` — `<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.DETECT_SCREEN_CAPTURE" />`, `Activity.ScreenCaptureCallback`, `registerScreenCaptureCallback(mainExecutor, cb)` in `onStart()`, `unregisterScreenCaptureCallback(cb)` in `onStop()`, per-activity scope, **"Only detects screenshots from hardware button combinations, not from ADB or instrumentation tests"**, the callback does not receive the image, and `FLAG_SECURE` prevents capture entirely; `about/versions/15/features` — `WindowManager.addScreenRecordingCallback()`, `SCREEN_RECORDING_STATE_VISIBLE`, `removeScreenRecordingCallback`
items.test:
For an app whose threat model includes remote-access-trojan scams — banking, crypto, brokerage —
the absence of both callbacks on the transaction screen is a missing control worth naming. Report it only
where you can also show a concrete capture succeeding.
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'DETECT_SCREEN_CAPTURE' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rnE 'registerScreenCaptureCallback|unregisterScreenCaptureCallback|ScreenCaptureCallback|addScreenRecordingCallback|SCREEN_RECORDING_STATE_VISIBLE' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# capture with the HARDWARE button combination, not adb -s "$SERIAL" — adb -s "$SERIAL" capture is documented as undetectable
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell input keyevent KEYCODE_SYSRQ   # or press Power+VolDown physically
```
items.proof:
A screenshot of the PIN or transfer-confirmation screen taken by the hardware combination, with
no app-side reaction — no blur, no warning, no session invalidation — on a screen that also lacks
`FLAG_SECURE`. **Do not use `adb shell screencap` as the PoC for this item**: the documentation states ADB
capture is not detected, so it proves nothing about the callback.
items.escalation: -> D20-038; -> D23 where the screen authorises a transaction.
items.ruled_out_when:
`FLAG_SECURE` is set on the screen (which makes detection moot), or the callback is
registered and the app visibly reacts to a hardware-button capture. Record the reaction.

items.title: Recents snapshot and the `FLAG_SECURE` family — the privacy framing that changes the rating
items.applies_to: all; **D04-042, D04-043 and D04-044 own the mechanics** — this item exists so the D20 pass does not re-derive them and so the privacy framing is recorded
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0289 (Runtime Verification of Sensitive Content Exposure in Screenshots During App Backgrounding — names the exact paths `/data/system_ce/0/snapshots` and `/data/system`), MASTG-TEST-0291 (References to Screen Capturing Prevention APIs), the three MASTG tests for `setRecentsScreenshotEnabled` not used, `SurfaceView.setSecure` not used and Compose dialogs' `SecureOn` not used (MASWE-0038) — **placeholders upstream with no published procedure, so test them by hand**; MASTG-KNOW-0053; MASTG-BEST-0014; MASWE-0038; semgrep rule `mastg-android-sensitive-data-in-screenshot`; deprecated predecessor MASTG-TEST-0010; AOSP threat [T.P4] "Screen unlocked (shared) devices under control of an authorized but different user"
items.test:
(D04-042/043/044 own the FLAG_SECURE mechanics and D11-039 the on-disk snapshot; this item owns only the privacy framing and the second rendering.) Run D04-042/043/044 once, then bring the result here and answer the only question that changes
the rating: **what data class is on that frame, and who picks up the device?** A balance on a personal
phone is P5. A patient record on a ward tablet, a PAN on a POS terminal, or a recovery phrase on any device
is a data-class argument that lifts the write-up out of `screen_caching_enabled`. Also check the three
gaps that sit *under* a correctly set `FLAG_SECURE`: a `clearFlags()` during a transition, a `SurfaceView`
(video, camera preview, map, PDF renderer) with its own secure flag, and a Compose `Dialog` whose window is
separate from the activity's — plus a fourth, **the second rendering**: every other screen, sheet, list row,
share preview, widget or notification that renders the same value, and the value's `contentDescription`. A
card screen that goes black proves nothing about the transaction-detail or share screen that draws the same PAN.

```bash
grep -rnE 'FLAG_SECURE|clearFlags\([^)]*FLAG_SECURE|setRecentsScreenshotEnabled|SurfaceView|setSecure\(|DialogProperties|SecureFlagPolicy|excludeFromRecents' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
# the second rendering: routes that set FLAG_SECURE vs every other binding site of the protected value (adapt the field names to the app's model class)
grep -rlE 'FLAG_SECURE' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | sort -u > "$E/logs/D20-040-secure-routes.txt"
grep -rnE 'setText\(|\.text = |contentDescription|Text\(' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | grep -iE 'cardNumber|pan|maskedPan|otp|balance|iban|seed|mnemonic|accountNumber' | grep -vFf "$E/logs/D20-040-secure-routes.txt"
# then drive each sibling route: adb -s "$SERIAL" exec-out screencap -p > "$E/screenshots/D20-040-<route>.png", and dump it (D20-042) for content-desc
semgrep --no-git-ignore --metrics=off -c "$MASTG_RULES/mastg-android-sensitive-data-in-screenshot.yml" $DEC/jadx/sources/ --json -o "$E/logs/D20-040-semgrep.json" && python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('$E/logs/D20-040-semgrep.json'));print('scanned',len(d['paths']['scanned']),'findings',len(d['results']))"
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell input keyevent KEYCODE_APP_SWITCH && adb -s "$SERIAL" exec-out screencap -p > recents.png
adb -s "$SERIAL" root && adb -s "$SERIAL" shell ls -la /data/system_ce/0/snapshots/ && adb -s "$SERIAL" pull /data/system_ce/0/snapshots ./snaps/
```
items.proof:
The pulled snapshot or Recents capture showing the value, **named by data class** —
"a full 16-digit PAN", not "sensitive data" — plus the shared-device or borrowed-device scenario the
client actually supports. For the second rendering: two captures of the same value — black on the protected
route, readable on the sibling — plus the sibling's node text.
items.escalation:
-> D04 for the mechanics and the differential evidence; -> D20-017/D20-018 for the
in-process capture that `FLAG_SECURE` does not stop; -> D11 because the snapshot is also a file on disk.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every screen carrying a credential, PAN, OTP, seed phrase or health datum produces a
black `screencap`, `screenrecord` refuses, and no snapshot file exists for the package after backgrounding
from those screens — and every binding site of each protected value is either on a `FLAG_SECURE` route or
masks/truncates the value, listed by route. Attach the black frame — it is one of the few visually provable
negatives here.

items.title: Framework single-surface rendering — one missing flag exposes the whole screen
items.applies_to: Flutter, Unity, and any engine rendering into a single `SurfaceView`/`TextureView`; also Cordova/Capacitor/RN where the WebView is the whole window
items.requires: device, flutter, unity, cordova, capacitor, react-native
items.maps_to: MASWE-0038 (its MASTG test for `setSecure` not used on `SurfaceView`s is a placeholder upstream)
items.test:
Native Android lets you protect a single activity. Flutter and Unity render every screen into one
surface on one host activity, so the protection decision is **all or nothing**: either the host activity
sets `FLAG_SECURE` (and the whole app becomes unscreenshotable, which product usually rejects) or nothing is
protected, including the PIN pad and the card form. Many teams resolve this with a plugin that toggles the
flag per route — test the toggle's timing, because a route transition is exactly where it fails.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn -E 'FLAG_SECURE|setSecure|SecureFlagPlugin|no_screenshot|flutter_windowmanager|ScreenProtector' $DEC/jadx/sources/ "$DEC/blutter/pp.txt" "$E/logs/strings.txt" 2>/dev/null | head   # the D19-034 Dart pool and the D19-009 Hermes string dump, by their canonical names
# capture at the transition, not at rest
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -n $PKG/.MainActivity
# navigate to the PIN route, then immediately:
adb -s "$SERIAL" exec-out screencap -p > t_pin.png
```

items.title: `uiautomator dump` — the on-screen text an accessibility-capable consumer reads
items.attacker: AM-04 (an enabled accessibility service; `uiautomator` itself is AM-11/AM-12 and is only the evidence tool)

items.test:
The underrated check. A screenshot proves a human can read the screen; a `uiautomator` dump proves
a **program** can read it, as structured text, without any image processing. Anything present as `text=` or
`content-desc=` in the dump is what an accessibility service or autofill consumer sees.

```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell uiautomator dump /sdcard/ui.xml && adb -s "$SERIAL" pull /sdcard/ui.xml
grep -oE '(text|content-desc)="[^"]*"' ui.xml | grep -inE '[0-9]{6}|[0-9]{12,19}|@|zq4h7m2kx9|balance|iban'
echo "nodes: $(grep -c '<node' ui.xml)"
```

UiAutomation clients (scrcpy, Frida sessions spawned with `-f`, test runners) and retry once; if it still fails,

`getRootInActiveWindow()` recursively and writing `className|text|contentDescription` per node to `poc.log`,

The card number, OTP, balance or personal datum present as readable `text=` in the node dump of a
sensitive screen, with the node count proving the dump succeeded.
items.escalation:

service via `AssistStructure`).

node text, or the node's text masked, with a non-zero node count proving the dump worked. Note that custom

items.title: Prove the cross-app clipboard read from a different UID — and state the mitigations honestly
items.attacker: AM-04 — a **foreground** app, or the default IME. **Background clipboard scraping is dead from Android 10; do not claim it.**
items.applies_to: **CURRENT** Android 10+ behaviour; LEGACY below that
items.maps_to: objection `android clipboard monitor`; drozer-modules `metall0id/post/clipboard.py` (`post.capture.clipboard`, `post.perform.setclipboard`) — MASTG-TOOL-0015, MASTG-TOOL-0029; T1414 Clipboard Data (ATT&CK: from Android 10, `ClipboardManager.OnPrimaryClipChangedListener()` *"can only be used if the application is in the foreground, or is set as the device's default input method editor (IME)"*); the drozer module is the historical reference — the PoC activity above is the reproducible path

different UID. Everything else is a description of the clipboard.

```
# objection, in-process (shows what the target writes)
android clipboard monitor
```
The cross-UID read comes from a zero-permission PoC app you build (drozer's `post.capture.clipboard` is a
community module installed from a remote index at run time — not reproducible enough for a report): one
foreground activity that reads `getPrimaryClip()` in `onWindowFocusChanged(true)` and writes the text to

focused app or the default IME; Android 12+ shows the user a "pasted from your clipboard" toast — say so):
```java
@Override public void onWindowFocusChanged(boolean f) {
  if (!f) return;
  ClipboardManager cm = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE);
  ClipData c = cm.getPrimaryClip();
  poc(this, "clip=" + (c != null && c.getItemCount() > 0 ? c.getItemAt(0).getText() : "null"));   // poc(): logcat + poc.log, as in D20-031
}
```
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -S -n <poc-pkg>/.ClipRead && adb -s "$SERIAL" pull /sdcard/Android/data/<poc-pkg>/files/poc.log "$E/logs/D20-044-poc.log"
```

next to the app's "Copied!" toast — and the PoC's (empty) permission list from `dumpsys package`, so the reader
can judge the precondition. Note in the report that the PoC was in the foreground (Android 10+ requirement).

items.ruled_out_when:

because the value was never placed there. Record the empty read alongside the "Copied!" toast.

items.title: Non-resettable hardware identifiers — IMEI, MEID, ESN, IMSI, build/SIM/USB serials
items.severity_note: Medium (High on an OEM engagement, where a platform restriction is bypassed)
items.vrt: `privacy_concerns.unnecessary_data_collection` (varies); if it becomes an auth factor, see D20-057
items.attacker: AM-08 (the recipient); AM-03 on an OEM build where a non-privileged app obtains a restricted value
items.applies_to: **Android 10+**: the restriction applies to **all devices regardless of target API level**. Apps targeting 10+ get a `SecurityException`; apps targeting 9 or earlier holding `READ_PHONE_STATE` get "`null` or placeholder data". **LEGACY:** below 10, `READ_PHONE_STATE` alone returned the real IMEI
items.maps_to: source.android.com `docs/core/permissions/immutable-device-ids` — restricted IDs are "telephony IMEI, MEID, ESN, and IMSI numbers, build, SIM, or USB serial numbers"; access limited to the default SMS app, privileged apps holding `READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE` **and** allow-listed in `privapp-permission.xml`, carrier-privileged apps, and device/profile owners with `READ_PHONE_STATE`; AOSP security-model threat [T.D1] "Abusing unique identifiers for targeted attacks … including using stable device identifiers to cross profile boundaries or factory resets"; MASWE-0068 (CWE-359); MobSF rules `api_get_device`, `api_get_subscriber`, `api_get_sim_serial`, `api_get_sim_provider`, `api_get_sim_operator`, `api_get_phone`; QARK `file/phone_identifier.py`; T1422 lineage via T1636
items.test:
Their presence in modern code means one of three things and you must say which: a legacy path
that now returns null, a privileged/carrier/DPC build that genuinely obtains them, or an OEM leak. Tying
any of them to a user account defeats the platform's identifier-resettability property, which is the point
of the restriction.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'getDeviceId\(|getImei\(|getMeid\(|getSubscriberId\(|getSimSerialNumber\(|getSimOperator\(|getLine1Number\(|Build\.getSerial\(|Build\.SERIAL' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -B4 -A4
grep -nE 'READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE|READ_PHONE_STATE|READ_PHONE_NUMBERS' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys package $PKG | grep -i READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell service call iphonesubinfo 1 2>/dev/null | head
# and where does it go?
IMEI=$(adb -s "$SERIAL" shell service call iphonesubinfo 1 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')
mitmdump -nr run.mitm --set flow_detail=3 2>/dev/null | grep -cE '[0-9]{15}'
```
items.proof:
A proxy capture containing a real IMEI / serial alongside an account identifier; or, on an OEM
build, a non-privileged app obtaining the value where Android 10+ should have thrown `SecurityException`.
items.escalation:
Cross-reset and cross-profile tracking — a stable supercookie for account linkage
([T.D1]). -> D25 for the OEM direction; -> D20-025 for the declaration mismatch.
items.ruled_out_when:
The getters exist only in a dead legacy branch guarded by a `Build.VERSION` check, the
app holds neither `READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE` nor carrier privilege, and the runtime call returns null or
throws — shown from a Frida hook on the getter, not just from the grep.

items.title: `ANDROID_ID` / SSAID and advertising-ID linkage to a persistent identity
items.vrt: `privacy_concerns.unnecessary_data_collection` (varies); a resettable advertising ID on its own is not a finding
items.attacker: AM-08
items.applies_to: all; `ANDROID_ID` before **Android 8.0 (API 26)** was a non-resettable, first-boot random value, while in recent versions it is unique per app-signing-key + user + device; an app targeting Android 13+ must declare `com.google.android.gms.permission.AD_ID` or it reads a zeroed advertising ID
items.maps_to: MASWE-0068 (Incorrect Use of Identifiers for User Tracking, CWE-359), MASWE-0067 (Lack of Anonymisation or Pseudonymisation Measures), MASWE-0074 (Inadequate Tracking Domains Declarations); MASVS-PRIVACY-2 — requires *"technical barriers when employing complex 'fingerprint-like' signals… a fingerprint used for fraud detection should be isolated and not repurposed for audience measurement in an analytics SDK"*; MobSF `api_get_advertising`; H1 **#803941** (NordVPN, Low, **$0**)
items.test:
The reportable shape is not "the app collects an advertising ID" — that is expected. It is
(a) the advertising ID transmitted **in the same request** as a persistent identifier or account id, which
breaks its reset guarantee; (b) the same identifier correlated across two unrelated third-party
destinations; (c) transmission after the user opted out of ad personalisation; or (d) a fraud-purpose
fingerprint reused for analytics, which MASVS-PRIVACY-2 calls out by name.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ANDROID_ID|Settings\.Secure\.getString|getAndroidId|AdvertisingIdClient|getAdvertisingIdInfo|isLimitAdTrackingEnabled|AppSetIdClient' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A6
# a class-name grep is confirmatory only: R8 renames library classes — the manifest provider/meta-data, string-literal and META-INF checks in D20-016 are the presence test
grep -nE 'com\.google\.android\.gms\.permission\.AD_ID' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
AID=$(adb -s "$SERIAL" shell settings get secure android_id | tr -d '\r')
mitmdump -nr run.mitm -s /dev/stdin <<PY
AID = b'$AID'
def request(f):
    b = (f.request.content or b'') + f.request.pretty_url.encode()
    if AID in b: print('ANDROID_ID ->', f.request.pretty_host, f.request.path[:70])
PY
# opt-out test: ad-personalisation opt-out / advertising-ID deletion is a Google Play services setting, not an AOSP secure setting (there is no limit_ad_tracking key)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -a com.google.android.gms.settings.ADS_PRIVACY      # Settings > Google > Ads: toggle 'Delete advertising ID' / opt out in the UI
# then verify the state the app sees before re-running the capture: hook AdvertisingIdClient.getAdvertisingIdInfo and expect isLimitAdTrackingEnabled()==true or id 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
```
items.proof:
One request containing **both** the advertising ID and a persistent identifier (Android ID,
account id, email hash), or the same ID reaching two distinct third-party destinations, or transmission
after the opt-out toggle.
items.escalation:
-> D20-025 (declaration); -> D20-020 (consent). Expect a Low rating unless the programme
scopes privacy explicitly — H1 #803941 paid $0 — so lead with the linkage, not the collection.
items.ruled_out_when:
The advertising ID is sent alone, never joined to a persistent identifier in the same
payload or across correlated requests, and transmission of the previous non-zero id stops after the Play
services opt-out (verified through the hook). Attach the before/after host and field lists.

items.title: Hardware MAC recovery through `/sys`, native code, or an OEM hook
items.attacker: AM-08; AM-03 on an OEM build
items.applies_to: **Android 10+** for default MAC randomisation; **11–13** for the progressive tightening
items.maps_to: AOSP security-model paper Table 3 — **11–13** "Restricted access to the hardware MAC address", mitigating [T.D1]; Table 6 — **10** "MAC randomization enabled by default for client mode, SoftAP, and Wi-Fi Direct", mitigating [T.P1][T.N1]; Table 3 — **10** "/proc/net limitations and other side channel mitigations"; §4.3.3 notes the `/proc` and `/sys` restrictions from Android 7/8 were partly motivated by apps abusing them "for side-channel attacks on data not otherwise accessible through their lack of required Android permissions (e.g. network hardware MAC addresses)"; MobSF `api_get_wifi`; MASWE-0068
items.test:
MAC randomisation removed a stable identifier deliberately. An app that recovers the **hardware**
MAC — through a native path, a `/sys` read, a privileged API or an OEM hook — has re-created it.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'getMacAddress\(|NetworkInterface\.getHardwareAddress|/sys/class/net|wlan0|getConnectionInfo\(' $DEC/jadx/sources/
for so in $DEC/apktool/lib/*/*.so; do strings -n 6 "$so" | grep -aE '/sys/class/net|wlan0|hw_addr' && echo "  ^ $so"; done
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell cat /sys/class/net/wlan0/address 2>&1     # expect permission denied from an app context
```
Compare the transmitted value against the real hardware MAC and against the per-network randomised one.
items.proof:
The app transmitting a MAC that matches the device's hardware MAC rather than the randomised
per-network value, shown in a proxy capture with both values side by side.
items.escalation:
Persistent cross-install tracking; on an OEM engagement it is a platform-restriction bypass
-> D25.
items.ruled_out_when:
No MAC-shaped value leaves the device, or the value transmitted changes when you forget
and rejoin the network (proving it is the randomised per-network MAC, which is the intended behaviour).

items.title: High-rate motion sensors as an inference channel
items.severity_note: High (undisclosed high-resolution motion telemetry is a documented keystroke and speech inference channel)
items.attacker: AM-08
items.applies_to: **targetSdk 31+** — Android 12 rate-limits motion sensors "to protect sensitive user information"; `HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS` lifts the limit

An app holding `HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS` without a stated high-rate use case (fitness tracking,

items.title: Installed-package enumeration as a fingerprinting surface
items.vrt: `privacy_concerns.unnecessary_data_collection` (varies) — and see the Graveyard: enumeration *as such* is documented intended behaviour
items.attacker: AM-08
items.applies_to: **LEGACY:** free package visibility is `targetSdk < 30`; from targetSdk 30 `<queries>` or `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES` is required
items.maps_to: Google Mobile VRP Invalid Reports, Intended Behavior: *"the ability of an application to tell which versions of which apps are installed is intended functionality of the Android platform which we do not consider a vulnerability"*; MobSF `api_installed`; MASWE-0066; MASWE-0068
items.test:
(This item owns only the 'list transmitted to a third party' proof; D03-046 owns the manifest/justification half and D01-043 restates it — record one verdict per half.) The installed-app list is a high-entropy, stable fingerprint. The finding is not "the app can
enumerate packages" — Google says that is intended — it is that the app **transmits** the list (or a hash
of it) to a third party as a tracking signal, while declaring `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES` with no stated need.
Note the second use of the same list: it is usually the app's root/Frida/competitor-detection blocklist,
which belongs to D21.
items.how:
```bash
grep -nE 'QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES|<queries>' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
python3 - <<'PY'
import re
m = open('$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml').read()
q = re.findall(r'<queries>(.*?)</queries>', m, re.S)
print('queries blocks:', len(q))
for b in q: print(b[:400])
PY
grep -rnE 'getInstalledPackages|getInstalledApplications|queryIntentActivities|getPackageInfo\(' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A4
mitmdump -nr run.mitm --set flow_detail=3 2>/dev/null | grep -cE 'com\.[a-z]+\.[a-z]+.*com\.[a-z]+\.[a-z]+'
```
items.proof:
A captured request containing a list (or a hash-set) of installed package names sent to a
third-party host, plus `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES` in the manifest with no feature that needs it.
items.escalation:
-> D03 (permission justification); -> D21 (the same list is the detection blocklist);
-> D20-025 (undeclared "Device or other IDs" collection).
items.ruled_out_when:
The manifest declares a narrow `<queries>` block matching specific, justified
interactions, no `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES`, and no package list leaves the device.

items.title: The identifier that *is* the authentication factor — the one that escapes a privacy rating
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (**P1**) where the identifier alone yields a session
items.attacker: AM-03 (any local app that can read or spoof the identifier) / AM-01 if it is accepted remotely
items.applies_to: all; common in legacy device-binding, "trusted device" and silent-login flows
items.maps_to: MASWE-0068; MobSF `api_get_device`; QARK `file/phone_identifier.py` — Google's guidance is to *"create UUID instead of using phone identifiers"*
items.test:
The inversion that pays. If `ANDROID_ID`, the advertising ID, the serial, a MAC or an
installation id is used as a **login key, a session key, or the "remember this device" token**, it is not a
privacy finding at all — it is a spoofable authenticator, because every one of those values is readable or
settable by code on the device and several are visible to other apps.
items.proof:
A session issued to a request carrying only the identifier, from a device that never
authenticated — the full request and the returned token, then one authenticated call with it.
items.escalation: This is a D13 report, not a D20 one. File it there and cross-reference.
items.ruled_out_when:
Identifiers appear only in telemetry payloads and never in an authentication or
session-establishment request, and a device-id-only call returns 401. Attach the 401.

items.title: EXIF geolocation not stripped — and the only variant with a rated VRT node
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.exif_geolocation_data_not_stripped_from_uploaded_images.automatic_user_enumeration` (**P3**) / `…manual_user_enumeration` (**P4**) — note the qualifier. **Without user enumeration there is no rated node**, and several programmes exclude EXIF by name
items.attacker: **AM-05** — another signed-in user of the same app, fetching a photo the victim uploaded
items.applies_to: all apps that accept and re-serve user photos: marketplace listings, dating profiles, review photos, claim evidence, support attachments
items.maps_to: Google Mobile VRP: *"Location information alone does not qualify (unless combined with the ability to uniquely identify an individual)"*; Basecamp lists "EXIF information not stripped from uploaded images" as out of scope; HackenProof excludes image metadata "unless they expose sensitive user information"; empirical: X/xAI "Twitter for android is exposing user's location to any installed android app" **$560**; T1430 Location Tracking; MASWE-0067
items.test:
The self-directed finding — "my own photo keeps its GPS" — is discounted everywhere. The payable
variant is cross-user: the app uploads photos with the GPS block intact **and the backend serves the
original file to other users**, so any viewer learns where the photo was taken. The "user enumeration"
qualifier in the VRT node is what you must satisfy: tie the coordinates to an identifiable person.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ExifInterface|TAG_GPS|setAttribute\("GPS|stripExif|removeExif|Bitmap\.compress|MediaStore\.Images' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# 1. make a photo with known GPS and upload it as account A
exiftool -GPSLatitude -GPSLongitude -Model -DateTimeOriginal test.jpg
# 2. fetch it as a DIFFERENT account
curl -s "https://cdn.target.example/listings/<id>/original.jpg" -H "Authorization: Bearer $B" -o got.jpg
exiftool -GPSLatitude -GPSLongitude -DateTimeOriginal -Model got.jpg
# 3. and unauthenticated, if the CDN allows it
curl -s "https://cdn.target.example/listings/<id>/original.jpg" -o anon.jpg && exiftool -GPSLatitude anon.jpg
```
items.proof:
`exiftool` on the file fetched **by a different account** returning the uploader's GPS
coordinates and device model, plotted to show they resolve to a residence, alongside the profile that
identifies the uploader. That pairing is the "user enumeration" the VRT node requires.
items.escalation:
Combine with the user-search oracle in D15 to turn "a listing" into "this named person's
home". Argue it up where the population is safety-sensitive — dating, gig workers, minors.
items.ruled_out_when:
The served file has been re-encoded or its metadata stripped — `exiftool` on the
fetched original returns no GPS tags — for every image endpoint (listing, avatar, message attachment,
support upload), tested individually. Different endpoints are often processed by different services;
check each.
