items.title: Data surviving logout and account switch
items.severity_note: Medium (High when the surviving artefact is an authenticator)
items.attacker: **AM-05** — another user of the same device, which the vendor supports for kiosks, POS terminals, ward tablets and family devices ([T.P4]) — AM-12 to observe (the root read of the sandbox is evidence, never the precondition)
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: H1 **#23913** (Twitter iOS — DMs surviving logout in the application-state file); H1 **#377582** (VK, Low 3.0 — cache DB obtainable by a third-party app); hackwithsingh sec-14-25 #54 "recent apps list", #55 "screenshot file residue"
items.test:
(Owner of the logout-residue test; D11-033 is its storage-chapter duplicate — run it here and record one verdict on both ids.) Log out, then diff. The question is not "is anything left" (something always is) but "is what is
left either an authenticator or content belonging to the previous user".
items.how:
```bash
AS 'ls -laR .' > before.txt                      # AS(): root read of the sandbox (## Items); run-as prints 'package not debuggable' on a release build
# ... log out ...
AS 'ls -laR .' > after.txt && diff before.txt after.txt
AS 'grep -rlEi "zq4h7m2kx9|token|bearer|@|[0-9]{12,19}" . 2>/dev/null' | head -30
AS 'find . -mtime -1 -type f' | wc -l            # -mtime, not GNU -newermt: toybox find has no date grammar
# server side
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $OLD" https://api.target.example/v1/me
# and the screen artefacts
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell ls /data/system_ce/0/snapshots/ 2>/dev/null
```
items.proof:
Message content, documents, cached PII or a token still present and readable after an explicit
logout — and, for the token, a 200 from the API with it.
items.ruled_out_when:
The post-logout diff shows every user-scoped file removed or overwritten, a grep for
the marker set returns zero across a non-zero file count, the old token returns 401, and the Recents
snapshot for the package is gone.

items.title: Account deletion that does not actually delete
items.severity_note: Medium as a privacy finding (High when deletion leaves a working authenticator)
items.attacker: AM-05 / AM-11 for the device side; the server side is a data-subject-rights failure — AM-12 to observe (the root read of the sandbox is evidence, never the precondition)
items.applies_to: all apps offering in-app account deletion — a Play requirement for apps with accounts
items.maps_to: VRT `insecure_os_firmware.failure_to_remove_sensitive_artifacts_from_disk` (CWE-459); MASVS-PRIVACY-4-flavoured data-deletion expectations; MASWE-0076 (Lack of Proper Data Management Controls); riya78 §7 "Analyze any cloud synchronization or backup mechanisms for data exposure"
items.test:
Delete the account, then check both ends. Server side: does `GET /me` 404, does the user still
appear in search, does the profile URL still render, do their messages still show in other users'
threads, does the data-export job still produce an archive? Device side: what remains in the sandbox and in
shared storage? Run this against a **throwaway account you own** — deletion is unrecoverable.
items.how:
```bash
# capture the "before" state for every surface you can reach
for E in /v1/me /v1/orders /v1/messages /v1/cards /v1/sessions /v1/export; do
  curl -s -o "before_$(basename $E).json" -w "%{http_code} $E\n" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $A" "https://api.target.example$E"; done
# delete
curl -i -X DELETE https://api.target.example/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $A"
# re-check with the SAME token, then from a SECOND account, then unauthenticated
for E in /v1/me /v1/orders /v1/messages; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} $E (own token)\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer $A" "https://api.target.example$E"; done
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} public profile\n" "https://target.example/u/<deleted-handle>"
curl -s "https://api.target.example/v1/search?q=zq4h7m2kx9" -H "Authorization: Bearer $B" | jq '.'
# device side
AS 'grep -rlEi "zq4h7m2kx9" . 2>/dev/null'       # AS(): root read of the sandbox (## Items)
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell ls -laR /sdcard/Android/data/$PKG /sdcard/Download 2>/dev/null
```
items.proof:
The deleted user's marker still returned by search under a second account, or the public profile
still rendering, or the cached PII still on the device — with the deletion confirmation screenshotted and
timestamped first.
items.ruled_out_when:
After deletion the own-token calls return 401, a second account's search returns
nothing for the marker, the public profile 404s, and the device grep returns zero. Record all four.

items.title: Deletion that does not revoke tokens, push registrations or third-party grants
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.failure_to_invalidate_session.on_logout` (**P4**); where the surviving token still reaches user data, `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (**P1**)
items.attacker: AM-05 / whoever holds a previously issued token
items.applies_to: all apps offering account deletion
items.maps_to: VRT `broken_authentication_and_session_management.failure_to_invalidate_session.*`; no external identifier verified in the corpus for the grant-revocation half
items.test:
Deletion usually flips a flag on a row. Enumerate everything that was issued in the account's
name and test each one after deletion: the access token, the refresh token, the FCM registration token,
OAuth grants the user made **through** the app to third parties, linked social identities, saved payment
instruments at the PSP, the support-chat identity, and any share links or invite tokens the account created.
items.how:
```bash
# capture every credential BEFORE deleting
ACCESS=$A; REFRESH=$(jq -r .refresh_token login.json); FCM=$(adb -s "$SERIAL" logcat -d | grep -oE 'token: [A-Za-z0-9:_-]{100,}' | tail -1)
# delete, then:
curl -i -X POST https://api.target.example/v1/auth/refresh -d "{\"refresh_token\":\"$REFRESH\"}" -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS" https://api.target.example/v1/orders
curl -i "https://target.example/s/<share-token-created-before-deletion>"
# push still deliverable?  (only to your own token, and say so in the report)
```
items.proof:
A refresh call returning a **new** access token after the account was deleted, or a share link
created by the deleted account still resolving, or a third-party OAuth grant still listed as active.
items.escalation:
-> D13. File this as an authentication finding with the deletion as the precondition; it is
the highest-severity item in the lifecycle group.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every captured credential returns 401/invalid_grant after deletion, share links 404,
and the third-party grant list is empty. Attach the refresh call's `invalid_grant`.

items.title: Uninstall / reinstall residue and Auto Backup restore
items.severity_note: High (when a session token survives uninstall — device resale or handover becomes ATO)
items.vrt: `mobile_security_misconfiguration.auto_backup_allowed_by_default` (**P5**); the escalation is `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (**P1**) via the restored token
items.attacker: AM-11 / AM-05 — AM-12 to observe (the root read of the sandbox is evidence, never the precondition)
items.applies_to: all. **`adb backup` is LEGACY** — from Android 12 (API 31) it no longer includes app data unless the app is debuggable, so report through the **Auto Backup / device-transfer** path and `<data-extraction-rules>` (which replaced `fullBackupContent` at API 31), or the report closes as non-reproducible
items.maps_to: hackwithsingh sec-14-25 #1 "data recovery after application uninstall", #17 "cloud backup (Google Drive)", #18 "auto-backup mechanism", #19 "device transfer mechanism", #20 "smart switch migration", sec-14-17 #49 "backup data is bound to device identity preventing cross-device restore abuse"; **D11-051 to D11-058 own the backup rig** — reuse it
items.test:
Uninstall and reinstall, then see what returns and what was left behind. Two distinct findings:
data that **returns** (Auto Backup restore of a token, so the app is logged in with no credentials
entered), and data **left behind** on shared storage that uninstall does not touch — including a third
shape: artefacts the app itself writes to shared media (MediaStore Images/Downloads) for a share, export,
print or receipt action, which uninstall does not remove and any `READ_MEDIA_IMAGES` /
`MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` holder reads (AM-04).
items.how:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" uninstall $PKG
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell ls -laR /sdcard/Android/data/$PKG /sdcard/Android/media/$PKG /sdcard/Download 2>/dev/null
adb -s "$SERIAL" install-multiple --no-incremental "$E"/apk/*.apk && adb -s "$SERIAL" shell monkey -p $PKG 1
AS 'ls -la shared_prefs/ databases/ files/'      # AS(): root read of the sandbox (## Items)
# the modern backup path (see D11 for the full rig)
grep -oE 'allowBackup="[^"]*"|fullBackupContent="[^"]*"|dataExtractionRules="[^"]*"|backupAgent="[^"]*"' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
cat $DEC/apktool/res/xml/backup_rules.xml $DEC/apktool/res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml 2>/dev/null
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell bmgr enabled; adb -s "$SERIAL" shell bmgr list transports; adb -s "$SERIAL" shell bmgr backupnow $PKG
# shared-media artefacts (share / export / receipt): find the writers, perform ONE such action, then query MediaStore by owner
grep -rnE 'MediaStore\.(Images|Downloads|Files)|RELATIVE_PATH|createWriteRequest|Environment\.DIRECTORY_(PICTURES|DOWNLOADS)|ACTION_SEND' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A4 | head -60
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell "content query --uri content://media/external/images/media --projection _display_name:relative_path:owner_package_name:date_added --where \"owner_package_name='$PKG'\""
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell "content query --uri content://media/external/downloads --projection _display_name:owner_package_name --where \"owner_package_name='$PKG'\""   # the device sh re-parses: the where-clause needs its own quotes there
```
D11-041 and D07-072 own the storage and provider mechanics — cross-reference them, do not re-derive.
items.proof:
The app opening straight into an authenticated session after a clean reinstall with no
credentials entered — record the whole sequence — or PII files still on `/sdcard` after uninstall, read
from a zero-permission PoC app; or a share/export artefact listed with `owner_package_name=$PKG`, read from
the probe app holding only `READ_MEDIA_IMAGES` (state the permission) and still present after `adb uninstall`.
items.escalation:
-> D11 for the backup mechanics and the restore-write direction; -> D13 for the restored
token; -> D02 if the build is debuggable and `adb backup` still works.
items.ruled_out_when:
`dataExtractionRules` excludes every credential- and PII-bearing path for **both**
`<cloud-backup>` and `<device-transfer>` (a missing section means that mode is fully enabled), a
`bmgr backupnow` + restore leaves the app logged out, and nothing remains under `/sdcard` after uninstall.

items.title: Camera or microphone access not tied to a visible user action
items.severity_note: Critical (covert recording); High for access that is disclosed but broader than necessary
items.attacker: AM-08 / the app itself
items.applies_to: Background sensor restriction is **Android 9+**; the status-bar indicator and global mic/camera toggles are **Android 12+**
items.maps_to: T1429 Audio Capture (ATT&CK: `RECORD_AUDIO` for the mic; `CAPTURE_AUDIO_OUTPUT` for call recording is *"restricted to privileged apps… only privileged applications, such as those distributed by Google or the device vendor, can access audio output"*, with `MediaRecorder.AudioSource.VOICE_CALL` as the call-capture source); T1512 Video Capture (`android.permission.CAMERA`; *"Android 9 and above restricts access to the mic, camera, and other device sensors from applications running in the background"*); T1541 Foreground Persistence; developer.android.com `about/versions/12/behavior-changes-all` (mic/camera toggles and indicators); MASTG-TEST-0254
items.test:
`appops` records a last-access timestamp per operation. Compare that record against your own
interaction log: any `RECORD_AUDIO` or `CAMERA` access in a window where you performed no
audio/video-related action is the finding. A concrete abuse worth testing on Android 12+: capture in very
short bursts, or starting while the screen is off, so the indicator is never meaningfully visible.
items.proof:
An `appops` access timestamp — or the Frida hook firing — during a window in which you performed
no related action, correlated with an audio/video artefact appearing in the data directory or an upload in
the proxy.
items.escalation:
-> D06 if a foreground service exists purely to keep the sensor alive (D20-066);
-> D20-025 for the declaration; -> D20-065 if the capture is also concealed.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every `appops` access timestamp aligns with a user action you performed, the hook never
fires while backgrounded, and the global toggle stops capture cleanly. Attach the `appops` timeline next to
your interaction log.

items.title: Concealment of collection — screen-off, muted device, invisible overlay
items.severity_note: High — deliberate concealment is a consent-integrity finding, not only a technical one
items.attacker: the app / an SDK inside it (AM-08)
items.applies_to: all
items.maps_to: T1628.002 User Evasion (ATT&CK: BRATA *"can turn off or fake turning off the screen while performing malicious activities"*; BusyGasper *"hide[s] malicious activity by turning the screen's brightness as low as possible and muting the device"*; Crocodilus S9004 *"has displayed a black screen overlay and has muted the sound of the device to conceal all malicious actions"*; Hornbill *"uses an infrequent data upload schedule to avoid user detection"*); T1628 Hide Artifacts
items.test:
Does the app suppress its own UI indications while collecting — a black or transparent overlay, a
muted stream, a suppressed notification, brightness driven to zero, or activity deliberately timed to idle
periods? In a legitimate app this usually surfaces as an over-aggressive analytics or session-replay
feature, so trace it to the SDK before writing it up as malice.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'setStreamVolume|ADJUST_MUTE|setAlpha\(0|alpha="0|TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY|setScreenBrightness|FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON|isInteractive|isScreenOn|PowerManager|SensorManager|setVisibility\(View\.INVISIBLE' $DEC/jadx/sources/
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys power | grep -iE 'mWakefulness|Display Power'
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys window | grep -iE 'TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY|alpha='
```
Record the screen while `dumpsys` shows the app active and the proxy shows uploads.
items.proof:
A recording in which the screen appears off or idle while `dumpsys` shows the app running and
the proxy shows outbound data, with the concealment call site named from the grep.
items.escalation: -> D18 (which SDK); -> D04 overlay findings; -> D20-064.
items.ruled_out_when:
No brightness, volume, overlay or visibility manipulation occurs outside a user-invoked
feature (a media player, a torch, a reader mode), and uploads are tied to foreground activity.

items.title: A foreground service held purely to keep sensor or capture access alive
items.attacker: AM-08 (the app itself, or an SDK inside it)
items.applies_to: targetSdk 34+ apps must declare an FGS type; `mediaProjection`, `microphone`, `camera` and `health` are the relevant ones
items.maps_to: T1541 Foreground Persistence; developer.android.com `develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types` (`HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS` as a manifest prerequisite for the `health` FGS type)
items.test:
Android 9+ blocks background sensor access, so an app that wants continuous access keeps a
foreground service alive. The finding is an FGS whose declared type exists only to hold the sensor or
projection open — a persistent notification the user reads as "syncing" while the real purpose is capture.
This is exactly ATT&CK's T1541 pattern.
items.how:
```bash
grep -nE 'foregroundServiceType|FOREGROUND_SERVICE(_[A-Z_]+)?' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rnE 'startForeground\(|ServiceInfo\.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A6
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys activity services $PKG | grep -iE 'foreground|type=|started|isForeground'
# does the sensor stay open across the service's lifetime?
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell appops get $PKG | grep -iE 'RECORD_AUDIO|CAMERA|time='
```
items.proof:
The FGS running with a `microphone` / `camera` / `mediaProjection` type across a window in which
the user performed no related action, with the `appops` timestamps showing continuous access and the
notification text describing something else.
items.escalation:
Report it together with D20-064 — the FGS is the *how* and the sensor access is the *what*.
-> D06 for the service-side findings, -> D03 for the permission set.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every FGS type declared corresponds to a user-visible, user-initiated feature, the
service stops when that feature ends (`dumpsys activity services` shows it gone), and sensor access stops
with it.

items.title: Run the pre-severity gate against the Critical claim, not against the leak
items.attacker: n/a
items.applies_to: every Critical or High claim in this chapter
items.maps_to: `triage-validation` PRE-SEVERITY GATE; the 7-Question Gate; the "never write *could potentially*" rule
items.test:
Write the draft Critical title first, then substitute the **Critical claim** — not the bug — into
each question. (1) Have I validated the full chain to attacker-attainable impact, or only one primitive in
the middle? "Token present in the log" is a primitive; "token in the log, read by package X, replayed
against the API returning the victim's data" is a chain. (2) What does the attacker walk away with, in one
concrete sentence? (3) Have I personally reproduced the whole chain end to end **at least twice**?
(4) Is there still an inheritance, signature, audience or binding check gating it? If yes it is not
Critical — document it as "primitive present" at a lower severity. (5) Has the programme rejected this
severity class before? For D20 specifically, question 5 usually answers itself: logging is excluded by
Google, EXIF by Basecamp, clipboard flattened to P5 by Bugcrowd.
items.how:
Fill the Q1 template before writing a word of the report: `1. Setup: I need [own account / a
co-resident app with notification access / no account] 2. Request: [the exact adb command, the exact HTTP
request, copy-paste ready] 3. Result: I can [read/modify] [exact data shown] 4. Impact: [ATO / PII read /
money] 5. Cost: [X minutes, $0]`. **If you cannot write step 2 as a real command or request, kill the
finding.** Then apply the writing rule: never "could potentially", "could be used to", or "may allow" —
either demonstrate the impact end to end, or downgrade the claim to match what you actually showed.
items.proof: A documented pass/kill decision per finding, and a severity that matches the demonstrated step.
items.escalation:
Where the VRT default undersells a demonstrated impact, open the report body with the
literal heading **"Severity request — please review carefully before applying VRT default"**, name the
chosen VRT and its default, state the priority you are requesting, and give three grounded impact axes —
one of which should cite the programme's own focus areas by name. Route within the system; never pick an
inaccurate VRT node to get a higher default.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — governance: complete when each Critical claim names the gate it passed, or carries the lower rating it fell to.

items.title: Retraction discipline, and the finding you must **not** retract
items.attacker: n/a
items.applies_to: every engagement
items.maps_to: `triage-validation` RETRACTION DISCIPLINE; `mid-engagement-ir-detection`
items.test:
Privacy findings are unusually prone to mid-engagement change: an SDK is remotely reconfigured, a
feature flag flips, a consent default is updated server-side. Two opposite rules apply and the difference
is whether you hold pre-change evidence.
items.how:
When a claimed finding fails reproduction and you have **no** pre-change evidence, retract it in
an appendix rather than silently dropping it:
```markdown
### Retracted: <finding name>
- **Original signal:** <what looked like a bug>
- **Disproving evidence:** <reproduction step + observation that disproves it>
- **Why it looked like a bug:** <root cause of the FP — marker collision, jitter, status-code-only confidence>
- **Retraction date:** <YYYY-MM-DD>
```
When a **confirmed** finding stops reproducing and you hold timestamped pre-patch evidence, **do not
retract it** — assume the client patched. Keep the finding with the timestamped capture, and note the
detection timeline itself as an observation about the client's response capability. A clean report with a
retraction appendix is more trustworthy than a longer one where findings fall apart at triage; a
self-retraction reads as a researcher who validates their own work.
items.proof: The appendix entry, or the timestamped pre-change capture.
items.escalation:
Retract pre-emptively if a submitted finding stops reproducing within 24 hours —
self-retraction does not hit the same platform-tracked metric a triager retraction does.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — governance: complete when every retraction names the mechanism that refuted the claim.

items.title: Chain-filing order for privacy primitives — file the primitive, then the consumer
items.attacker: n/a
items.applies_to: every multi-finding engagement; D20 produces primitives more often than consumers
items.maps_to: `bugcrowd-reporting` §5 (chain filing) and §8 (submission-order strategy)
items.test:
Almost everything in this chapter is a primitive whose severity comes from a consumer in another
domain: the logged token (consumer: D13 session replay), the notification OTP (consumer: D13 2FA bypass),
the accessibility-readable confirmation screen (consumer: D13/D23 automated transaction). File in the order
that lets you reference real identifiers.
items.how:
(1) Identify the highest-severity chained outcome. (2) File each primitive as a separate report at
its honest standalone severity — typically P4/P5 here — leaving a placeholder cross-reference line.
(3) File the chain consumer with the full narrative at the chained severity, filling in the real primitive
IDs. (4) Edit each primitive to backfill the consumer's ID. The consumer body carries:
```markdown
## Chain partners (filed as separate reports)
- **submission [UUID-1]** — [primitive 1: e.g. session token written to logcat]
- **submission [UUID-2]** — [primitive 2: e.g. OEM package holding READ_LOGS on the supported device set]
These primitives have independent fix surfaces and are filed separately per the programme's
"one fix = one bounty" rule.
```
**Do not** paste the whole chain narrative into every primitive, claim each primitive is independently P1,
or ask for a single combined bounty — a chain is a **severity amplifier, not a merge request**. And do not
file everything within minutes of each other: triagers read a simultaneous batch as low-effort spam.
items.proof: Cross-referenced IDs in both directions.
items.escalation: n/a.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — mechanics: complete when each primitive is filed before its consumer and every consumer report cites it.

items.title: The five-screenshot pattern adapted to a data-leak PoC
items.attacker: n/a
items.applies_to: every D20 finding with a demonstrated consumer
items.maps_to: `evidence-hygiene` §7 (the five-screenshot state-change pattern); MHL's quantified-exfiltration reporting standard
items.test:
A leak PoC needs the same five-shot discipline as a state change, remapped: (1) **pre-state** —
the value inside the app, shown as the user sees it, with your marker visible; (2) **the leak itself** —
the capture, log line, notification dump or request body containing that same marker, from the consumer's
side; (3) **negative control** — the same capture taken *before* the value existed, or from an app/account
that should not see it, showing the marker absent; (4) **positive post-state** — the value used, e.g. the
token replayed against the API returning the victim's data, or the OTP completing the login;
(5) **side effect** — whether the app or the backend noticed: a notification email, a session-list entry,
an audit-log line, or their absence.
items.how:
Name files `{finding-#}-step{n}-{description}.png` (`04-step2-notification-listener-otp.png`) and
reference them by filename in the body. Take all five in one sitting — reloading regenerates cookies and
invalidates the earlier captures. Quantify rather than describe: MHL's report-ready lines are the standard
to match — *"Call returned 679091 bytes / Found 63 PNG image(s) in protobuf / Permissions used: NONE"*, and
for a contacts exfil, *"EXFILTRATED name #1..3 / EXFILTRATED phone #1..3 … all of the above was read
WITHOUT READ_CONTACTS"*.
items.proof:
Five numbered, cross-referenced artefacts, with counts and byte totals instead of adjectives,
and the attacker app's permission set stated explicitly (ideally empty) — triagers look for that line.
items.escalation:
Pair with D20-006 (the PII mask/leave-visible split) before attaching anything, and with
D20-005 (redact at capture time). For a Critical or High claim, reproduce with a second tool as well: the
same leak shown through both a Frida hook and an independent capture is much harder to argue with.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — evidence: complete when each data-leak finding carries the five screenshots this item lists.

items.title: Shortcut and conversation donations put account data on launcher, share-sheet and widget surfaces — and keep it after logout
items.severity_note: Low standalone (labels on the device holder's own surfaces); Medium when the previous account's contacts, numbers or messages survive logout or account switch on a shared-device-supported app, or a third-party launcher reads them
items.attacker: AM-05 / AM-11 (the next user of a shared device after logout); AM-04 for a third-party launcher the user made the default HOME app
items.applies_to: apps publishing dynamic, pinned or long-lived sharing/conversation shortcuts (`ShortcutManager` API 25+; sharing shortcuts API 29+; `pushDynamicShortcut` and `removeLongLivedShortcuts` API 30+); AppSearch donations are D11-075
items.maps_to: MASWE-0036 (Unnecessary Exposure of Sensitive Data via the User Interface), MASWE-0077 (Inadequate Data Visibility Controls); CWE-359; developer.android.com `develop/ui/views/launch/shortcuts` (dynamic, pinned, `pushDynamicShortcut`), `training/sharing/direct-share-targets` (sharing shortcuts, `setLongLived`), `reference/android/content/pm/LauncherApps` (`getShortcuts`, served to the default launcher only), `reference/android/content/pm/ShortcutManager` (`removeAllDynamicShortcuts`, `removeLongLivedShortcuts`); D11-075 (AppSearch cross-app read); D04-071 (widget and lock-screen rendering)
items.record: `logs/D20-071.txt` (the grep and the `dumpsys shortcut` block before and after logout); `screenshots/D20-071-<n>.png` (launcher long-press, share sheet, widget)
items.skip_when:
`grep -rlE 'ShortcutManager|ShortcutInfo' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | wc -l` prints 0 and
`grep -c 'android.app.shortcuts' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml"` prints 0 (framework class names survive
R8) — write `n/a — D20-071: 0 ShortcutManager/ShortcutInfo references in $DEC/jadx/sources, no android.app.shortcuts meta-data`.
items.test:
Shortcuts are copies of app data the system stores and renders outside the app: dynamic and pinned
shortcuts on the launcher's long-press menu and home screen, long-lived sharing/conversation shortcuts in the
system share sheet's Direct Share row, the Conversations section and the conversation widget, and — through
`LauncherApps.getShortcuts` — in whatever third-party launcher the user set as HOME. The finding is a label or
person carrying account data (contact names, account, booking or card numbers, balances) that survives logout
or account switch because the app never calls `removeAllDynamicShortcuts()` / `removeLongLivedShortcuts()`, or
that a third-party launcher receives.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ShortcutManager|ShortcutInfo|setShortLabel|setLongLabel|setPerson|setLongLived|pushDynamicShortcut|setDynamicShortcuts|addDynamicShortcuts|removeAllDynamicShortcuts|removeLongLivedShortcuts|requestPinShortcut' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | tee "$E/logs/D20-071.txt"
grep -rlE 'google\.shortcuts|firebase\.appindexing' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | head -3   # a hit: donations also go to an SDK index — attribute it in D20-019
# logged in as A, after the flows that create shortcuts (chats, recent items, saved payees): the D20-002 canary must appear
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys shortcut > "$E/logs/D20-071-before.txt"; grep -c zq4h7m2kx9 "$E/logs/D20-071-before.txt"   # positive control: > 0
# log out (then log in as B), and repeat
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys shortcut > "$E/logs/D20-071-after.txt"; grep -c zq4h7m2kx9 "$E/logs/D20-071-after.txt"
```
Then long-press the launcher icon, open any app's share sheet and check the conversation widget picker, and
screenshot each. If `before` is 0 while the launcher visibly shows the canary, this image masks labels in
`dumpsys`: the screenshots are the evidence. For the third-party-launcher half, a PoC HOME activity (`cmd package set-home-activity
<poc-pkg>/.Home`) calls `LauncherApps.getShortcuts()` with `FLAG_MATCH_DYNAMIC | FLAG_MATCH_PINNED |
FLAG_MATCH_CACHED` for the target package and writes every field it actually receives to `poc.log` — the
platform withholds the launch intent from launchers, so report only what the log shows.
items.proof:
The canary (a planted contact or payee name from D20-002) in `dumpsys shortcut` and on a
screenshot of the launcher menu, share sheet or widget **after** logout or account switch, next to the
`before` count; or the PoC launcher's `poc.log` line holding it.
items.escalation:
-> D20-060 (record the same residue there); -> D04-071 (widget and lock-screen surfaces);
-> D09-040 (a pinned shortcut whose retired route still resolves); -> D11-075 for AppSearch documents.
items.ruled_out_when:
Labels carry no account data (generic "New chat", "Scan"), or the app clears dynamic and
long-lived shortcuts on logout and account switch — the canary count drops from `before` > 0 to `after` = 0 —
and the PoC launcher's log holds only generic labels.

items.title: Delegate-process blind spot: egress from the SDK Runtime sandbox or a delegate package is invisible to in-process hooks
items.severity_note: Support (decides the attribution column of every egress item; rated nowhere on its own)
items.vrt: n/a — method; the attributed flow is rated in D20-019 / D20-025
items.attacker: n/a (tester method)
items.applies_to: apps declaring `<uses-sdk-library>` (runtime-enabled SDKs run in the SDK sandbox process on Android 14+ devices) or handing payments, identity, analytics or model inference to another package's service
items.maps_to: developer.android.com `design-for-safety/privacy-sandbox/sdk-runtime` (sandbox process with its own UID; `SdkSandboxManager.loadSdk`), `guide/topics/manifest/uses-sdk-library-element`; D01-084 (SDK Runtime declarations), D01-041 (process topology), D11-074 (the delegated store)
items.record: `logs/D20-072.txt` (process list, bindings, per-UID socket census for each UID)
items.skip_when:
`grep -c '<uses-sdk-library' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml"` prints 0, no `sdk_sandbox`
process exists while the flow runs, and D01-041 names no other package handling a sensitive flow — write
`n/a — D20-072: no uses-sdk-library, no sdk_sandbox process during the flow, no delegate package in D01-041`.
items.test:
Before an egress table is believed, establish which process opens each socket. A runtime-enabled SDK
runs in the SDK sandbox process under its own UID, and some apps hand a sensitive flow to another package's
bound service. Frida hooks and stack traces in the app's process (D20-003/009/019/022/024) see none of that
traffic: a thin client then reads as "no third-party egress" while the delegate ships the identifiers — and,
the other way round, delegate traffic gets filed against the app.
items.how:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell ps -A -o USER,UID,PID,NAME | grep -E "sdk_sandbox|$PKG" | tee "$E/logs/D20-072.txt"     # run while the flow is live
grep -nE '<uses-sdk-library' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml" | tee -a "$E/logs/D20-072.txt"
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys activity services | grep -nE "ServiceRecord|$PKG" | tee -a "$E/logs/D20-072.txt"   # read which other package's ServiceRecord lists a binding from $PKG
# then run the D20-019 per-UID socket census once per UID: the app's, the sandbox's (UID column above) and each delegate package's
```
Proxy flows are attributed the same way: the per-UID census and the request's User-Agent or SNI decide the
origin process, never the app's in-process hook.
items.proof:
The D20-019 host table with an "origin process" column — app UID, sandbox UID or delegate package —
each row backed by its census lines.
items.escalation:
Delegate in scope -> run D20-019 / D20-025 against its flows; out of scope -> mark the affected
D20 rows `blocked` with `needs: scope decision on <delegate package>` (never `n/a`); -> D18-061 (what the SDK
could do in-process, which a sandboxed SDK loses); -> D11-074 (where the delegate stores the data).
items.ruled_out_when:
No `sdk_sandbox` process and no binding to another package exist while the flow runs (the
`ps` and `dumpsys` lines are the negative), or every established socket in the census during the flow belongs
to the app UID — with the app UID's own connections present as the control that the sampling worked.

items.title: Content Capture: PIN, OTP and card views handed to the system content-capture service without an opt-out
items.severity_note: Low (privacy hardening: the reader is a system service the OEM ships); Medium only where the programme's scope names on-device data minimisation and a credential or OTP view reaches the service
items.vrt: varies — no dedicated node; rate as `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies) only when the captured secret resurfaces to another reader
items.attacker: AM-11 (the captured text resurfacing in a user-visible system feature on a shared device); n/a for the system service itself
items.applies_to: Android 10+ (API 29) device images whose OEM configures a content-capture service; apps whose secret views do not set `importantForContentCapture`
items.maps_to: MASWE-0036 (Unnecessary Exposure of Sensitive Data via the User Interface); CWE-359; developer.android.com `reference/android/view/contentcapture/ContentCaptureManager` (`setContentCaptureEnabled`), `reference/android/view/View#setImportantForContentCapture(int)` (`IMPORTANT_FOR_CONTENT_CAPTURE_NO_EXCLUDE_DESCENDANTS`); AOSP `android.service.contentcapture.ContentCaptureService` (the CTS test service is the PoC shape); D28-034 / D28-035 (assistant surfaces that consume screen structure)
items.skip_when:
the device API is below 29, or `adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys content_capture` shows no
service for user 0 on every device image in scope — write `n/a — D20-073: no content-capture service on
<device image> (dumpsys content_capture: <line>)`.
items.test:
On Android 10+ the content-capture service the OEM configures receives a structured stream of the
view text of every package it allow-lists, unless the app opts views out (`android:importantForContentCapture="no"`
/ `noExcludeDescendants`, `View.setImportantForContentCapture`) or disables capture with
`ContentCaptureManager.setContentCaptureEnabled(false)`. The question is whether PIN, OTP, PAN, balance and
message views reach it. Whether password-type fields and `FLAG_SECURE` windows are excluded is decided by the
experiment on the device image in scope, not assumed.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'importantForContentCapture|setImportantForContentCapture|IMPORTANT_FOR_CONTENT_CAPTURE|setContentCaptureEnabled|ContentCaptureManager' "$DEC/jadx/sources" "$DEC/apktool/res/layout" | tee "$E/logs/D20-073.txt"
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys content_capture | tee -a "$E/logs/D20-073.txt"    # the bound service and its allow-list: is $PKG captured on this image?
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell cmd content_capture help                                  # print this image's grammar before using it
# userdebug AVD, for a candidate you will report: bind a PoC service temporarily (the CTS pattern), then type the D20-002 canaries
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell cmd content_capture set temporary-service 0 <poc-pkg>/.CaptureService 120000
```
The PoC service (declared with `android:permission="android.permission.BIND_CONTENT_CAPTURE_SERVICE"`, built
against the system API surface) allow-lists the target in `onConnected()` and writes each
`onContentCaptureEvent` view node's text to `poc.log`. Type into a benign field (search) first: that line is
the positive control.
items.proof:
The PoC service's `poc.log` holding a PIN, OTP or PAN canary from the target's view with the
target's package on the session; or, statically, a secret view with no opt-out on a device image whose
`dumpsys content_capture` allow-lists the package — reported as static, with that line.
items.escalation:
-> D28-034 / D28-035 (assistant and screen-reading surfaces fed the same structure);
-> D20-048 (autofill: the parallel `ViewStructure` path that `importantForAutofill` governs separately).
items.ruled_out_when:
Secret-bearing views or their container set `importantForContentCapture="no"` /
`noExcludeDescendants`, or the app disables content capture — or the PoC service, holding its positive-control
line from the benign field, receives none of the canaries.

items.title: Device-fingerprint signals joined to an account identifier in one payload
items.severity_note: Low standalone (a signal inventory is not a finding); Medium when five or more stable device signals travel with an account identifier or email to a third-party host, or a fraud fingerprint is reused for analytics or ads
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies) for the joined record reaching a third party; Privacy Concerns › Unnecessary Data Collection (varies) while it stays first-party
items.attacker: AM-08 (the third-party SDK or host that receives the joined record)
items.applies_to: all; most visible in apps bundling device-intelligence, fraud, analytics or ad SDKs
items.maps_to: MASVS-PRIVACY-2; MASWE-0068 (Incorrect Use of Identifiers for User Tracking), MASWE-0067 (Lack of Anonymization or Pseudonymisation Measures); CWE-359; D20-053 (identifier linkage), D20-019 (attribution)
items.test:
Reading `Build` fields is ordinary; the finding is the join. Many stable device attributes —
`Build.FINGERPRINT`/`BOARD`/`HARDWARE`/`BOOTLOADER`, display metrics, the sensor list, fonts, battery, carrier,
time zone and locale, `ANDROID_ID` — assembled into one record and sent with an account identifier, email or
advertising ID form a re-identification key that outlives an advertising-ID reset. The second shape is a
fingerprint collected for fraud prevention and reused by analytics or ad hosts, the isolation MASVS-PRIVACY-2
asks for.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnoE 'Build\.(FINGERPRINT|BOARD|HARDWARE|BOOTLOADER|HOST|DISPLAY)|getDisplayMetrics|getSensorList|BatteryManager|getNetworkOperatorName|getSimOperator|ANDROID_ID|TimeZone\.getDefault' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 | tee "$E/logs/D20-074.txt"   # files reading many signals = the collectors
mitmdump -nr run.mitm -s /dev/stdin <<'PY'
import re
SIG = [rb'(?i)"?(model|manufacturer|brand|board|hardware|bootloader)"?\s*[:=]', rb'(?i)"?fingerprint"?\s*[:=]', rb'(?i)screen|density|dpi',
       rb'(?i)timezone|"tz"', rb'(?i)carrier|operator|mcc', rb'(?i)battery', rb'(?i)sensor', rb'(?i)font', rb'(?i)android_?id', rb'(?i)locale|language']
ACCT = [b'zq4h7m2kx9', b'15550137742']          # the D20-002 canary email / phone
def request(f):
    b = f.request.content or b''
    n = sum(1 for s in SIG if re.search(s, b))
    if n >= 5: print(f.request.pretty_host, f.request.path[:50], 'signals=%d' % n, 'ACCOUNT-ID' if any(a in b for a in ACCT) else '')
PY
```
Run the D20-024 inflate pass first: device-intelligence payloads are usually compressed or encoded.
items.proof:
One request body (inflated) holding five or more device signals together with an account
identifier or canary, to a host attributed to its SDK (D20-019), next to the privacy policy / Data safety text
that does not disclose device-fingerprint collection or that host.
items.escalation:
-> D20-053 (reset the advertising ID and show the record still links the account); -> D20-025
(declaration delta); -> D21 when the same fingerprint is the fraud control (the remediation is isolation, not removal).
items.ruled_out_when:
No request joins five or more stable signals with an account identifier, or the joined
record goes only to the first-party fraud endpoint the privacy policy names for that purpose and no analytics
or ad host receives it — the D20-019 attribution table shows which hosts do.
